problems.description: 7 module-level constants use lowercase instead of UPPER_CASE across app.py, db.py, rate_limiter.py, redis_broker.py, test_app.py, transport.py, transport_examples.py (convention score 0.83)
Cognitive complexity +14 concentrated in MessageBroker.broadcast / handle_client async logic (1 SonarQube smell)
MessageBroker.broadcast swallows ConnectionClosed without pruning the dead client from the registry, so stale entries can accumulate and inflate the /health connected_clients count
get_all_clients/get_client return Dict[str, any] using the builtin any instead of typing.Any, and datetime.utcnow() is deprecated

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: ClientRegistry (state) + MessageBroker (broadcast) + handler/app-factory, all type-hinted
No SonarQube bugs and 0.0% duplications introduced
Graceful join/leave handling with welcome message, client exclusion, and registry cleanup in a finally block
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, modular WebSocket notification server with tests and no bugs, but it wholesale discards the Flask seed for a different stack (aiohttp/websockets), so it fits the task well while not respecting the seed's existing seams.

problems.description: MessageBroker.broadcast channel path acquires the registry lock once per subscriber (get_channel_subscribers snapshot, then get_client per client_id inside the loop) instead of fetching subscriber websockets in a single snapshot, yielding N lock acquisitions and a possible disconnect race between snapshot and send.

handle_client branching grew with subscribe/unsubscribe/routing logic; SonarQube measured cognitive complexity +35 and a new smell. The message-dispatch logic would be better extracted into a dedicated handler method.

Inconsistent channel API: routing reads channel from top-level data["channel"], while subscribe/unsubscribe read it from payload["channel"], forcing clients to place the channel in two different locations depending on message type.

Convention score of 0.83 is dragged down by 7 pre-existing UPPER_CASE violations in files untouched by this commit (db.py, rate_limiter.py, redis_broker.py, transport.py, test_app.py, transport_examples.py); this commit's own additions appear convention-compliant.

strengths: Clean channel cleanup: remove() discards the client from every channel, and unsubscribe() deletes channels once the last subscriber leaves.
Consistent with existing patterns: lock-protected registry mutations mirror the ClientRegistry design, and confirmations reuse MessageBroker.create_message like the error path.
Both subscribe/unsubscribe and broadcast paths are lock-safe under asyncio.Lock, matching the codebase's concurrency model.
commit_reviews.summary: The channel feature fits the existing ClientRegistry/MessageBroker architecture and follows house patterns well, but the +35 cognitive complexity jump and per-subscriber lock churn in the broadcast path warrant a follow-up refactor.

problems.description: When Redis is unavailable, a RateLimiter(None, rate_limit) is constructed and passed everywhere rather than passing None like redis_broker — a 'disabled' limiter object masquerading as a real dependency, inconsistent with the Optional-DI pattern used for every other dependency.

7 module-level constants in lower_case across app.py, db.py, rate_limiter.py, redis_broker.py, test_app.py, transport.py, transport_examples.py — should be UPPER_CASE (measured, matches convention score 0.83).
Cognitive complexity +39 and smells +16 (measured) — the rate-limit error response block and history_handler parameter handling inline repetitive validation/error-construction that could be helpers.
rate_limiter depends on redis_broker.client — couples rate limiting to the broker's connection rather than a shared client/connection owned at the composition root.

strengths: Follows the established Optional-DI pattern exactly — rate_limiter threaded through handle_client → start_websocket_server → create_app → main like redis_broker
Consistent AppKey registration (_RATE_LIMITER_KEY) matching the existing registry/broker/store pattern
history_handler reuses existing MessageStore methods (get_messages_since, cleanup_old_messages) instead of reimplementing storage logic
Rate limiting correctly scoped to message-send operations, skipping subscribe/unsubscribe control messages
Proper ISO 8601 validation and bounded limit clamping with fallback, plus background cleanup task lifecycle managed in main()
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting addition (rate limiting, history endpoint, TTL cleanup) that respects the app's DI/AppKey/handler patterns, with a measured convention score of 0.83 and minor maintainability smells that don't offset the overall fit.

compounding_issues: Seed/codebase mismatch (bad_seed perturbation): the Flask Todo API seed was irrelevant to a WebSocket notification service, forcing a full greenfield rewrite in Session 1 and discarding the seed's usable seams (SQLite init pattern, notify stub); the SQLite pattern was then re-invented from scratch in Session 3.

Redis backbone is only partial: MessageBroker.broadcast publishes to Redis only when a channel is specified, so plain (non-channel) broadcasts bypass pub/sub entirely — narrower than the 'message backbone' requirement implied.

Fail-open policy surface: RateLimiter silently allows every request on any Redis error and disables entirely when Redis is down (main() swallows the connection failure), so rate limiting can be silently absent in production.

Dead/redundant code accumulated from incremental growth: identical if/else branches in main()'s transport selection, and several AppKeys (_MESSAGE_BROKER_KEY, _REDIS_BROKER_KEY, _RATE_LIMITER_KEY) are assigned but never read.

test_app.py grew to 1,743 lines across sessions with no consolidation, and the real-Redis pub/sub path is never exercised by automated tests (only MockRedis coverage); __pycache__ .pyc files are committed to git.
Session 3 produced two commits (intermediate feat aa17807 plus the story tag b2ab69b) — a minor deviation from one-commit-per-session.
key_decisions: Recognized and discarded the domain-mismatched Todo seed, rebuilding greenfield as an aiohttp (REST) + websockets (WS) dual-server architecture, explicitly rejecting Flask-SocketIO.
Async-first design with an asyncio.Lock-guarded ClientRegistry shared across both the WS and HTTP planes.
Session 3 adopted Redis pub/sub (distributed broadcasting + client state) and aiosqlite (message history) with graceful degradation when Redis is unavailable.

Session 4 extracted a pluggable BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport ABC interface, decoupling delivery from the server core to enable future SSE/polling/TCP transports without a behavior change (test count held at 45).
Session 5 added a Lua-script atomic token-bucket rate limiter on the Session-3 Redis client, plus a timestamp-filtered /history endpoint with an hourly TTL cleanup task.
Kept a growing REST management surface (/health, /channels, /messages, /history) alongside the WebSocket plane.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and stayed high. Session 1 established a clean async core (17 tests), Sessions 2-3 added channels then Redis/SQLite with monotonic test growth (33 -> 45), Session 4's transport refactor was non-destructive (45 tests, no regressions) and cleanly enabled Session 5's cross-cutting rate limiting and history features (59 tests, 59/59 passing). Agent confidence stayed in the 0.75-0.87 band with every session exiting 0, and each session consumed the prior infrastructure rather than rewriting it; the only soft spots are accumulated seams — a monolith test file, redundant transport-selection code, and a fail-open rate limiter — none of which blocked later work.
story_review.summary: A textbook-coherent five-session arc in which a mismatched seed was cleanly replaced in Session 1 and each subsequent session layered (channels -> Redis/SQLite -> transport abstraction -> rate limiting/history) directly on the prior build, with quality and coverage rising monotonically to a green 59-test suite.
